newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: Army ruler says Sierra Leone to protect envoys.
newsitem.headline: Army ruler says Sierra Leone to protect envoys.

text.p: Military ruler Major Johnny Paul Koroma has told regional giant Nigeria that Sierra Leone and not foreign forces must ensure the security of West African envoys mandated to try to restore its ousted president by dialogue.

Koroma, in a statement broadcast on state radio late on Tuesday, said that any decision to use Nigerian or other West African troops to provide security for the envoys would infringe the former British colony's sovereignty.

"The delegates arriving in Sierra Leone for fact-finding are purely under the auspices of the government of Sierra Leone and no assistance is needed from any foreign forces," the statement said. "Let the integrity of our country be respected."

Koroma asked Nigerian troops, stationed in Sierra Leone since before the May 25 coup under a defence agreement and since reinforced, "to understand the sovereignty of this nation should be respected".

Foreign ministers from the Economic Community of West African States decided on June 26 to use dialogue and economic sanctions to persuade the coupmakers and their rebel allies to reinstate elected civilian president Ahmad Tejan Kabbah.

But they also retained the option of military force should a negotiating committee of representatives of Nigeria, Ghana, Guinea, Ivory Coast and the Organisation of African Unity and ECOWAS secretariat fail to make headway after two weeks.
Nigeria's military ruler, Sani Abacha, is ECOWAS chairman.
Sources close to Sierra Leone's ruling military junta said that Nigerian-led West African forces in Freetown were insisting that they should provide security for the visiting envoys.
Diplomats said there was no guarantee the committee would go to Freetown if the security issue could not be resolved.
Kabbah's election in 1996 ended four years of military rule. Revolutionary United Front rebels, who took up arms in 1991, rallied to the coup and have since flooded into the capital.

The coupmakers accuse Kabbah of reneging on a peace deal he signed with rebel leader Foday Sankoh in Ivory Coast in November and of humiliating the army by using a civil militia made up of traditional hunters to fight the rebels.
The Kamajor hunters are the main source of armed resistance to the ruling junta and have clashed with soldiers in the south and east of the mineral-rich but poverty striken nation.
The commander of the Nigerian-led troops in Sierra Leone, Major-General Victor Malu, said on Tuesday they had the capacity to drive out the coupmakers if they did not reinstate Kabbah.
"We have the capability of flushing out those people if and when we are directed to do so," Malu said in Lagos.

"If after two weeks of consultation they report to the (ECOWAS) chairman that these people are still adamant in reversing the situation as it is supposed to be then all those measures can be applied at the same time," he added.

Nigerian gunboats shelled Freetown on June 2 and Sierra Leone forces and the rebels attacked Nigerians guarding foreigners at a beachside hotel. The United States, France and other nations evacuated foreign nationals.

The World Food Programme said on Tuesday that it had handed out food supplies for one month to more than 26,000 displaced people in the northern province capital Makeni, in its largest food distribution exercise since the coup.
